The word straits (noun) has two distinct meanings — one concrete and geographical, one figurative and emotional. Both are rooted in the same underlying idea: something narrow and tight, with little room to move.
Meaning 1: A Narrow Body of Water

A strait (or straits) is a naturally formed narrow strip of water that sits between two landmasses and connects two larger bodies of water. It is nature's corridor — land pressing in from both sides, water flowing through the middle.

Examples:

  • The Strait of Gibraltar — a slim passage of water between Spain (Europe) and Morocco (Africa), connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea. If you can picture a bottleneck between two continents, that's a strait.
  • The Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman. Nearly 20% of the world's oil passes through it, making it one of the most strategically important straits on Earth.
  • The Bering Strait — the narrow stretch of water between Alaska and Russia. So narrow that the two countries are only about 85 km apart at this point.
  • The Straits of Magellan — the waterway at the southern tip of South America, famously navigated by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520.

What makes a strait different from other bodies of water?

  • A strait is natural — it was created by geography, not dug by humans (a man-made version is called a canal).
  • It is narrow — that is its defining feature.
  • It connects two larger bodies of water — it links, not separates.

Singular vs. Plural: Both strait (singular) and straits (plural) are used for the geographical meaning. Some waterways use the singular in their name ("Strait of Gibraltar"), while others use the plural ("Straits of Malacca"). This varies by convention and doesn't change the core meaning.
Meaning 2: A Situation of Difficulty or Hardship

In everyday language — especially in common phrases — straits means a condition of serious difficulty, hardship, or distress. It almost always appears in the plural form in this sense.

Think of it this way: just as a geographical strait is a tight, hemmed-in passage with land pressing in from both sides, a figurative "strait" is a tight, hemmed-in situation in life — where you feel boxed in, with limited options and no easy way out.

This meaning is used most often for financial difficulty, but it can describe any situation of serious trouble or desperation — a business on the verge of collapse, a country in a political crisis, a person with no good options left.

Examples in sentences:

  • "After the factory closed, thousands of workers were left in straits."
  • "The startup burned through its funding in six months and found itself in dire straits."
  • "Following the drought, farmers across the region were in desperate straits."

These are the phrases where straits (in its figurative meaning) most commonly appears:

1. In dire straits
This is the most widely used phrase. Dire means extremely serious or terrible. So "in dire straits" means in a situation of extreme, urgent difficulty — things are very bad, possibly close to collapse or ruin.

  • "The hospital is in dire straits — it may have to shut down within months due to lack of funding."
  • "He had spent all his savings and was in dire straits."

You may also know this as the name of the famous British rock band Dire Straits — they named themselves after this phrase.

2. In desperate straits
Similar to dire straits, but emphasizes urgency and desperation — the person or organization is running out of time or options.

  • "Refugees fleeing the war were in desperate straits, with no food, water, or shelter."

3. In difficult straits
A softer version — describes a challenging but not necessarily catastrophic situation.

  • "The small business found itself in difficult straits after losing its biggest client."

4. In straitened circumstances
This is a formal, slightly old-fashioned phrase specifically meaning in a state of financial difficulty or poverty. It is used to politely say that someone is struggling with money.

  • "After the business failed, the family lived in straitened circumstances for years."
  • "Many retired teachers found themselves in straitened circumstances due to inadequate pensions."

These two words sound identical when spoken, but they are spelled differently and mean completely different things. This is one of the most common errors in English.

  • Strait / Straits → narrow waterway, or a difficult situation
  • Straight → not curved; direct; without bends ("a straight line," "go straight ahead")

So when someone says "in dire straits," they mean difficulty (strait), not a straight line. The spelling strait always carries the meaning of narrowness or tightness.
Related Words That Share the Same Core Idea

Knowing these will make the word family click for you:

Straitjacket
A jacket with very long sleeves that are tied behind a person's back to restrain their arms — used historically to confine people who were considered violent or dangerously unstable. The garment tightly confines you, leaving no freedom of movement. This is the geographical "tight passage" idea applied to the body.

It is also used figuratively to mean anything that overly restricts freedom of thought or action:

  • "The rigid bureaucracy acted as a straitjacket on innovation."
  • "These outdated laws are a straitjacket on economic growth."

Straitlaced
Describes a person who is very strict, rigid, prim, or conservative in their morals and behavior — someone who follows rules tightly and is uncomfortable with looseness, informality, or deviation from convention. Imagine someone "laced up" so tightly they cannot loosen up.

  • "She was too straitlaced to laugh at the joke."
  • "He grew up in a straitlaced household where even casual dress was frowned upon."
The One Idea Tying It All Together

Every use of straits — whether a narrow waterway, a financial crisis, a straitjacket, or a straitlaced person — comes back to the same central image: something narrow, tight, and confining, with very little room to move. Once you hold that image in your mind, the word and its entire family become intuitive.

• Geographical straits → a narrow natural waterway connecting two larger bodies of water (e.g., Strait of Gibraltar, Bering Strait)
  • Figurative straits → a difficult, tight, or desperate situation, especially financial hardship
  • Most common phrase → in dire straits (in very serious trouble)
  • Don't confuse → strait (narrow/difficult) with straight (not curved)
  • Related words → straitjacket (physical or figurative confinement), straitlaced (strict, rigid person), straitened circumstances (financial hardship)
